english_translation: Close the door firmly when you leave the house.

dialogue.shona: Vhara musuwo zvakasimba kana uchibuda mumba.
dialogue.english: Close the door firmly when you leave the house.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Vhara [close! / shut!] • musuwo [door / doorway] • zvakasimba [zvakasimba] • kana [if / when / or] • uchibuda [uchibuda] • mumba [in the house / indoors]

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Vhara')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'Vhara' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakasimba')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakasimba' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('mumba')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'mumba'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Household Cooperation, Politeness & Consideration at Home
cultural_notes.content: Daily home life in Shona culture revolves around mutual assistance ('kubatsirana') and consideration for others in the household. When asking a family member to help lift something heavy ('undibatsire kusimudza'), open or close a door ('musuwo') or window ('hwindo'), or speak softly ('kuzevezera') while a child is sleeping ('mwana akarara'), polite phrasing keeps household life warm and harmonious.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'There is a cup of water on the table' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Patafura' ('on the table') pairs with 'pane' ('there is at/on that spot') + 'kapu yemvura' ('a cup of water').

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Ndasiya nharembozha yangu pachigaro mumba yokutandarira.'
options: Please close the door and all the windows before sleeping.
I left my mobile phone on the chair in the living room.
My keys are inside the small bag on the table.
We are sitting under the shade tree outside the house.
active_exercises.correct_answer: I left my mobile phone on the chair in the living room.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Ndasiya' = 'I left', 'nharembozha yangu' = 'my mobile phone', 'pachigaro' = 'on the chair', 'mumba yokutandarira' = 'in the living room'.

active_exercises.prompt: Why do we say 'miti mitatu' for 'three trees' but 'zvigaro zvitatu' for 'three chairs'?
options: Because trees are taller than chairs
Because 'mitatu' means thirty and 'zvitatu' means three
The number stem '-tatu' takes 'mi-' for 'miti' (trees) and 'zvi-' for 'zvigaro' (chairs)
Because 'miti' is singular and 'zvigaro' is plural
active_exercises.correct_answer: The number stem '-tatu' takes 'mi-' for 'miti' (trees) and 'zvi-' for 'zvigaro' (chairs)
active_exercises.explanation: Numbers 1–5 mirror the prefix of the noun they count: 'miti mitatu', 'zvigaro zvitatu', 'vanhu vatatu'.
